summary: Japan's northernmost national park: the volcanic cone of Mount Rishiri rising straight out of the Sea of Japan, Rebun, the low island of flowers beside it, and the peat bogs of the Sarobetsu Plain on the Hokkaido coast opposite. Climb Rishiri, walk Rebun's clifftop meadows in early summer, or watch migrating geese over the largest lowland raised bog in Japan.
story: Mount Rishiri is a single volcanic cone, 1,721 metres high, that makes up almost the whole of its island about twenty kilometres off the Hokkaido coast. It was built in the late Pleistocene; seen from the mainland it seems to float on the sea, and it is also known as Rishiri Fuji. Rebun, the island to its north-west, is lower and quite different in shape: hills that end in sea cliffs, with stacks such as Momoiwa, the 'peach rock', standing above the shore.

The islands' isolation and cold maritime climate let alpine plants grow almost at sea level, and some grow nowhere else. Rebun's meadows flower from late spring through summer, and its Rebun atsumorisō, a creamy lady's-slipper orchid, is protected as a nationally rare species and grows in only a few places on the island. On Rishiri the yellow Rishiri poppy flowers in the summit gravel in July and early August and is found on no other mountain.

Across the strait, the Sarobetsu Plain was once a lagoon. Rivers filled it over thousands of years with silt and dead vegetation, and the peat that built up became the largest raised bog in lowland Japan. Along the coast at Wakasakanai and Bakkai, lines of dunes run parallel to the sea with ponds and oak and fir woods between them. Bean geese and other waterbirds stop on the plain on their spring and autumn migrations, and in early summer the bog turns yellow with Ezo daylilies.

People here have always lived from the sea. The waters around both islands produce Rishiri kombu, a kelp prized across Japan, and in summer it is spread to dry along the beaches; sea urchin is harvested under a catch limit. On the plain, peat was dug for fuel and soil improver until 2002, and the old workings are now being restored. Rishiri and Rebun became a quasi-national park in 1965 and were raised to a national park, with Sarobetsu added, in 1974.
howItWorks: The park is spread across six municipalities — Wakkanai, Toyotomi and Horonobe on the mainland, and Rishiri, Rishirifuji and Rebun on the islands — and like all Japanese national parks it is a set of zones laid over land with many owners. Of its 24,512 hectares, 20,119 are national land, 1,542 public and 2,851 private. The park takes in much of both islands as well as the coastal dunes and bog on the mainland, and since 2021 two marine park zones covering 3,356 hectares protect stretches of the surrounding sea.

Some 9,566 hectares are special protection zone, where picking any plant, collecting fallen leaves or branches, catching animals or lighting a fire all need a permit from the Minister of the Environment. Most of the rest is special zone, where building, felling and quarrying need a permit and listed alpine plants may not be picked; only 155 hectares is ordinary zone. For a visitor that means staying on the boardwalks and trails: the bog and the flower meadows are easily damaged by trampling, and orchids such as the Rebun atsumorisō are additionally protected under the law on endangered species.

The Sarobetsu Plain is also a Ramsar wetland, registered in November 2005, and the peat cuttings worked until 2002 are the site of a nature-restoration project. The Ministry runs its northern work from a ranger office in Wakkanai, and the two mainland visitor centres — the Sarobetsu Wetland Center in Toyotomi and the Horonobe Visitor Center — are the places to ask about conditions on the plain.

sights.name: Mount Rishiri (利尻山)
sights.note: A 1,721-metre volcanic cone climbed from Oshidomari on the north coast or Kutsugata on the west. A long, eroded climb for experienced hikers.

sights.name: Himenuma (姫沼)
sights.note: A small pond in the woods on Rishiri's north side, circled by a short path with the mountain reflected in it on still days.

sights.name: Otatomari-numa (オタトマリ沼)
sights.note: Rishiri's largest pond, about a kilometre round, on the south-east coast, with a path round it and the mountain reflected in it.

sights.name: Momodai-Nekodai viewpoint (桃台猫台展望台)
sights.note: On southern Rebun, looking at the 250-metre Momoiwa and the Nekoiwa stack, near the flower-lined Momoiwa trail.

sights.name: Cape Sukoton (スコトン岬)
sights.note: Rebun's northern tip, looking out to Todo-jima where sea lions haul out. The start of the clifftop trail by Cape Gorota and Cape Sukai.

sights.name: Rebun atsumorisō colony (レブンアツモリソウ群生地)
sights.note: A slope in northern Rebun where boardwalks pass close to the island's rare cream-coloured lady's-slipper orchid.

sights.name: Panke-numa (パンケ沼)
sights.note: The largest lake on the Sarobetsu Plain, eight kilometres round and stained red by iron from the peat, with Rishiri on the horizon.

sights.name: Hamayūchi (浜勇知園地)
sights.note: A dune-coast stop on the road south of Wakkanai, with daylilies and water lilies in early summer and Rishiri across the sea.

sights.name: Sarobetsu Wetland Center
sights.note: On the raised bog in Toyotomi, with a boardwalk loop of about a kilometre through daylilies, cranberry and sundews.

sights.name: Horonobe Visitor Center
sights.note: Exhibits and films on how the Sarobetsu bog formed, with an upstairs deck looking towards Rishiri. Closed November to April.

entrances: Oshidomari, Rishiri's main ferry port and the start of the Oshidomari route up the mountain
Kutsugata, on Rishiri's west coast, for the Kutsugata route and the Mikaeridai viewpoint
Kafuka, Rebun's ferry port on the south-east coast
Sarobetsu Wetland Center and Horonobe Visitor Center, on the mainland plain
planYourVisit.reservations: No reservation is needed to enter the park. Taking a car on the ferry is expensive, and island buses are few, so many visitors book a bus tour on the islands; check ferry and bus timetables before you go.
permits: No permit is needed to climb Mount Rishiri or walk Rebun's trails; plants may not be picked anywhere in the special zones
camping: A campground on Rishiri's lower Oshidomari route, near the Kanro Sensui spring
lodging: Wakkanai, for the ferries and the northern end of the plain
seasonalClosures: Horonobe Visitor Center closes from November to April
Mount Rishiri usually has its first snow at the beginning of October; the routes are for experienced hikers only outside summer

weather: Summer this far north is short and cool. The Ministry recommends June to September for Mount Rishiri, whose summit usually takes its first snow at the start of October. Rebun's flowers bloom from late spring through summer, and the Sarobetsu daylilies from late June into early July. Spring and autumn bring migrating geese to the plain. In winter Rishiri draws back-country skiers, and the Ministry recommends going with a guide.
directions: Fly from Tokyo Haneda to Wakkanai (about two hours), or take a train or highway bus from Sapporo (around five and a half to six hours). Ferries run from Wakkanai Port to Oshidomari on Rishiri (about 1 hour 40 minutes) and Kafuka on Rebun (about 1 hour 55 minutes). Rishiri also has a small airport with flights from Sapporo's Okadama Airport, and seasonal ones from New Chitose. Island buses are infrequent; bus tours or hired bicycles are the usual way round. A car is the easiest way to reach the Wakasakanai coast and the Sarobetsu Plain on the mainland.

chronology.text: Eruptions build the cone of Mount Rishiri.
Rishiri and Rebun are designated a quasi-national park on 10 July.
Rishiri-Rebun-Sarobetsu National Park is designated on 20 September, adding the Sarobetsu Plain.
Peat digging on the Sarobetsu Plain ends.
The Sarobetsu Plain is registered as a Ramsar wetland of international importance.
Two marine park zones are designated in the seas around the islands.

safety: Rishiri has no resident brown bears — one that swam across in 2018 was the first recorded on the island since 1912 — but higuma live on the Hokkaido mainland opposite. On the mainland side, make noise when walking and keep food sealed.

Mount Rishiri's trails are steep and badly eroded near the top, with loose scree and a narrow summit ridge, and rescue calls from the mountain are frequent. The climb is a long day on an isolated peak in the open sea; turn back in wind or cloud.
Ferries and island flights are cancelled in rough weather. Leave slack in your plans, especially outside summer.
regulations: Stay on the boardwalks on the Sarobetsu Plain and at the atsumorisō colony; the bog and the meadows are damaged by trampling.
Do not pick, dig up or buy wild-collected plants. The Rebun atsumorisō is a nationally designated rare species and taking it is a crime.
Picking any plant or collecting fallen branches in the special protection zone needs a permit from the Minister of the Environment.
